title: Sleep in peace
hook: the eleven blessings of metta, read whole

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahapajapati's brief teaching, and your line, where does this lead?. Did you catch one urge toward more? Today closes the week, and it ends, fittingly, at bedtime. Day six hundred seventy-two.

This week was full of tools for ordinary life. Five ways to remove a grudge. Food that gives life. Pulling your ears when you nod off. The eight winds. The goldsmith's scale. And toward less. Now the last sutta of the week, from the final book of the Numbered Sayings, the Book of Elevens. It's a list of what happens to a person who practices loving-kindness, metta, steadily: developed, cultivated, made a vehicle and a foundation, the text says, well established and well undertaken. There are eleven blessings, and today we read the whole list. Today: metta.
screen: `A WEEK OF TOOLS.` → `THE BOOK OF ELEVENS.` → `ELEVEN BLESSINGS, WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in order. One: you sleep easily. Two: you wake easily. Three: you don't have bad dreams. Four: you are dear to human beings. Five: you are dear to non-human beings. Six: the devas, the gods, protect you. Seven: fire, poison and weapons don't touch you. Eight: your mind becomes concentrated quickly. Nine: your face is bright and clear. Ten: you die unconfused. Eleven: if you go no further in this life, you are reborn in the Brahma world. Notice where the list starts. Not with heaven. With sleep. The first three blessings are about the night, the place where resentment and worry do their best work, replaying the day at two in the morning. A heart that's practiced goodwill has less to replay. Then the list moves outward, to people, to unseen beings, to protection; then inward, to concentration and a clear face; and finally to the very end, dying without confusion. It's a whole life, from tonight's pillow to the last breath. Some of the blessings, like fire and poison not touching you, are read by some teachers literally, as the power of a mind full of kindness, and by others as describing a life that makes fewer enemies. The text itself simply lists them. And notice how this ties the week together. Grudges removed, winds passing, less wanting: all of it makes for a quieter night.
screen: `SLEEP EASY, WAKE EASY.` · `DEAR TO HUMANS AND NON-HUMANS.` · `A QUICK MIND, A BRIGHT FACE.` · then, large: `DIE UNCONFUSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer metta before sleep. You can do it now, or save it for your pillow tonight. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind yourself, and wish yourself well, in a few simple words: may I be well, may I rest. Then someone you love. Then someone neutral, a face you passed today. Then, if you can, someone from this week's grudges. Then everyone, everywhere, going to sleep tonight. Let the words get softer as you go. The bell holds the time.
metta. The Pali word for loving-kindness, the practice behind the eleven blessings in the Book of Elevens, a list that runs from an easy night to an unconfused death and beyond. Today's word.
Your line: wish one person well. Tonight, as you lie down, wish one person well, then yourself, and let that be the last thought of the day. Day six hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: In some Theravada communities the eleven blessings of metta are chanted in Pali, and metta meditation, wishing well to oneself and then widening circles of beings, is a common practice before sleep.

fork.setup: of the eleven blessings of metta, which comes first in the list?
fork.reveal: sleep comes first. the list starts with tonight's pillow and ends with dying unconfused.

original.note: Pali metta: loving-kindness, goodwill; from mitta, friend. Sanskrit maitri.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving-kindness is a nice feeling with no practical effect.
what it means: AN 11.16 lists eleven blessings, starting with sleep and ending with death.
what a scholar hears: the list is introduced with a stack of verbs, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle and a basis, to show it describes steady practice, not a passing mood.

notes: AN 11.16 paraphrased. Confirm the order of the eleven, especially 'devas protect' (6) and 'fire, poison, weapons' (7). Some editions number this AN 11.15.
The literal vs. figurative reading of blessing 7 is presented as a range of teachers' views; confirm fair.
Confirm the full list of verbs in the introductory formula.
The practice uses 'may I be well, may I rest' as simple well-wishing phrases, not a quoted prayer; confirm acceptable.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'the very end of the Numbered Sayings' changed to its final book (11.16 is not the last sutta); cut 'you may have heard one or two'; 'many teachers' to 'some teachers'; the word line no longer implies the list ends at death (it ends with the Brahma world); softened 'many' in howItsDone.
